newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Child rebel fighters cut off eastern Zaire town.
newsitem.headline: Child rebel fighters cut off eastern Zaire town.

text.p: Rebel fighters, many of them child warriors, were reported on Monday to have cut off the eastern Zairean town of Bunia defended by up to 5,000 Zairean troops.

The U.N. refugee agency meanwhile said about 15,000 Rwandan refugees abandoned their camps in northwest Tanzania on Sunday, defying a Tanzanian government campaign to repatriate them following the return of more than 500,000 from eastern Zaire.
In the eastern Zairean town of Beni, aid officials said rebels spearheaded by Mai-Mai tribal witchcraft fighters had cut off the key town of Bunia, 140 km (85 miles) northeast of Beni.
"The Banyamulenge have surrounded Bunia with Mai-Mai," said Mustafa Lufungula, local operations head of the Zaire Red Cross.

"The Mai-Mai children tell us what is going on, because they trust us, and because we look after them when they are wounded," he added. "The Banyamulenge are using them because of their supposed magic powers, they are taking advantage of them."
Local officials said on Sunday the rebels and their Mai-Mai allies had taken two strategic towns, blocking routes for Zairean troops in Bunia to the regional centre of Kisangani to the west.
The rebels say Bunia is their next target on the northern front as they extend the area they carved out of eastern Zaire in the past seven weeks.

Residents of Beni said the frontline was about 20 km (12 miles) from Bunia, which has a strong garrison of Zairean government troops put by the rebels at 5,000 men, some pushed north by the rebel advance and some flown in as reinforcements.

The rebel advance since seizing a strip of territory running 520 km (320 miles) north-south along Zaire's border with Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi has slowed in the past week amid signs that Zaire's ill-disciplined army was more determined to resist.

Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril, the Canadian commander of a multinational force for central Africa, said on Sunday the rebels assured him aid agencies would have access to any Rwandan refugees in need. But most are outside rebel-held territory.
Speaking after talks with rebel leaders, Baril said he found the rebel-held area more secure than during his previous visit.
"But there's still a lot of conflict going on and we expect the humanitarians (U.N. and other agencies) will have trouble reaching people because of the conflict," the general added.

Many aid agency workers are scathing about the inactivity of the multinational force, which has a headquarters in the Ugandan capital Kampala but cannot deploy in eastern Zaire for political and security reasons.
The force's mission was complicated by the return of more than 500,000 Rwandan refugees from eastern Zaire last month and problems in finding hundreds of thousands of others who fled north and west.

Peter Kessler, a spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), said on Monday most of the 15,000 Rwandan refugees who left their camps in northwestern Tanzania on Sunday had headed north and northeast, away from the Rwandan border.
The exodus was in reaction to a UNHCR-Tanzanian government plan to repatriate all the 542,000 Rwandan refugees in Tanzania by the end of the month.

Kessler said it was hard to guess why the refugees fled but he linked their movement into the bush to the presence in camps of the Interahamwe, the Rwandan Hutu militia which holds sway in the camps and has intimidated refugees against returning home.
"They (the Interahamwe) have been knocking on every hut, terrorising the refugees with scare stories about the situation back home," he said. Aid workers confirmed the scare campaign.

The Interahamwe was the moving force behind the massacre of up to one million Rwandan Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda in 1994. Many of them fear going home because they might face prosecution for their part in the genocide of Tutsis.
The human rights group Amnesty International has criticised the plan as forced repatriation.
